**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell you not to start a startup while you're in college. The one exception is that if your side project takes off by itself, he'd say it's reasonable to run with it.

He holds that you can't be a student and a founder at once, and that waiting costs you nothing because you're more likely to succeed later.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed this directly in 2014 and again, less directly, in 2026.

**Why he'd say it**
- **It's about the label.** "you can't start up a startup as a student, because if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." ([Before the Startup, 2014](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1102s) @ 18:22)
- **His advice at your age is blunt.** "Do not start a startup in college." And: "though starting a startup could be a good thing to do at some point, 20 is not the optimal time to do it." (same talk, [@ 18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s))
- **Waiting is free.** "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." (same talk, [@ 21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s))
- **Your early twenties are for open-ended exploration.** He says to "plunge deeply into projects on a whim that seem like they have no payoff," because success takes the serendipity out of your life ([@ 19:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1172s)).
- **Your side project is the exception.** "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." (same talk, [@ 21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s)) His example is Facebook.
- **The 2026 essay keeps the rule but leans on the exception.** In [How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html) he writes: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." He also says many student side projects are "incipient startups" and notes Microsoft and Meta both began during Harvard's reading period. If one takes off, "it's either that or drop out."

**What this means for you**
- **Keep building the project, but don't treat it as a startup yet.** His rule for ideas is to work on side projects and let a startup idea emerge, not to hunt for one. Early on, he says to build something you and your friends want.
- **Use the free time to learn.** His two-word advice to young would-be founders is "just learn" ([@ 30:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1849s)). He also says to study CS and other hard skills and to skip business school.
- **The real test is users.** If people are pulling the project out of your hands, that's the Facebook case, and you'd then face a choice between abandoning it and dropping out. He doesn't say which to pick.

**What would change his answer:** the project taking off without you pushing it. Traction from real users turns it from a hobby into the exception he allows. Being "unsure whether you can do it" doesn't count: for that he says the only way to find out is to try, "just not now" ([@ 23:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1438s)).

**Caveats**
- His firm "do not" comes from a 2014 talk to Stanford students. The 2026 essay is addressed to universities, not to you, and doesn't say outright what a student should do. His emphasis has shifted toward letting side projects become startups, but he hasn't reversed the rule.
- In the same Q&A he says "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it," which pulls against waiting. The vault doesn't show him resolving this.
- He runs Y Combinator, which funds founders, so he has a stake in how people think about starting up.
- He says elsewhere that you can't tell in advance whether you're cut out for it.

**Verdict:** Yes. Paul Graham says you should go to Silicon Valley, but "for a bit and then come back" is enough. He said this in a talk to a Stockholm audience, so your city came up directly.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high)

**Why he'd say it**
- He gave your exact question a direct answer: "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([talk @ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s), [[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]])
- **Peers:** "You get the best peers. And in fact, the talent pool expands in two dimensions. The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." (@ 1:09)
- **Serendipity:** "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." (@ 3:20)
- **Speed:** "Things also tend to move faster in the big centers because the people are better, they're more confident, and that's more decisive." (@ 3:53)
- **The effect on you:** he calls this the biggest advantage. "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." (@ 8:19) And: "When you're a big fish in a small pond, you don't even know how big a fish you are." (@ 8:52)
- **Fundraising:** Valley investors decide faster than European ones because competition punishes waiting. Going there also raises your standing with investors back home ([[fundraising/investors/why-valley-investors-decide-faster]]).

**Coming back is fine, and he encourages it.** He says: "as long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub." (@ 16:10) Returning founders bring better startups, Valley money and Valley culture. He thinks Stockholm could become a hub, since "All you need is a place founders want to live and a critical mass of them." (@ 21:09) He doesn't say staying in Stockholm for good is wrong, but he clearly wants you to spend time in the Valley first.

**Caveats**
- He admits he's biased: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book." He runs YC, which profits from founders coming over. He says the best way to do the "go and come back" trip is to do YC.
- He also reports that YC startups that go home are only about half as likely to become unicorns. He discounts this himself for selection bias and for the higher valuations in the Bay Area. The vault shows no numbers or method behind it.
- Sam Altman (July 2026) agrees but less firmly. He says YC's rule that founders move to San Francisco was clearly right and is probably still good advice. He says he has less of an intuition for it now ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]]).

**What would change his answer:** I found nothing in the vault where he says to stay put. The nearest thing is his remark that money isn't everything once you have kids (@ 19:30), which he makes about going home. Even then his advice is to go for a stint rather than skip the Valley.

**My own view, kept separate:** The Valley case is strongest for pure software startups that need a fast-moving investor and peer network. If your customers and team are in Europe, the cost of a long stay is higher than his talk admits.

**Verdict:** Stop polishing and take fewer meetings. Spend the time making the company grow fast enough that investors chase you. Months of pitching and follow-ups is the pattern Seibel calls a waste.

**Based on:** said it. The Oct 2026 episode with Dalton Caldwell covers this situation closely (confidence: high).

**Why he'd say it**
- Time on the deck is time not spent on the company. "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 10:03, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s))
- Investors chase the deals that matter. He asked investors what share of their deals they chase versus get through the front door, and the answers ranged from 80/20 to 90/10 in favor of chasing. The job is to become a company they chase.
- A strong company needs little deck. When Socialcam was the number two app, "one of our pitch decks kind of just was like here's some questions you can ask us." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 9:30, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=570s))
- Traction beats pitching skill. Caldwell says, and Seibel agrees (they credit PG with the idea): "it's way better to be like a very bad fundraiser ... with something that's working than someone that's a very good fundraiser with ... something that's not working at all." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 5:35). PG said the same in 2014: "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning ... growing fast, and then simply tell investors so." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 9:51)
- Long, open-ended meetings are often investors keeping an option open. The hosts say VCs mostly invest on traction, so they keep meeting you in case you take off, and the meetings make that less likely. The vault doesn't attribute that point to Seibel by name, so treat it as the hosts' joint view. Seibel does call the wasted time "a drag on the industry" ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:44).

**What he's done:** At Justin.tv he spent about eight months failing to raise. With two months of runway left, the team turned to making the company profitable. He says they got more done in those two months than in the months of pitching ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:44).

**What he'd tell you to do now**
1. Treat months of meetings with no term sheet as a signal that you lack leverage. Don't treat it as a pitch problem.
2. Put the deck down. Build and grow, then go back with a growth graph and proof points.
3. Cap the time you give fundraising. Keep a few investors warm with short updates showing growth.
4. Keep working on your sales pipeline. This is adapted from his sales advice, not a fundraising quote: one deal you badly want to close makes you stop filling the funnel ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 12:51).

**What would change his answer:** If you're already growing fast and investors are asking to move quickly, raise and close fast. The advice is aimed at a raise that has dragged on without leverage.

**Caveats from the vault:**
- Caldwell co-hosts the show, and his fund, Standard Capital, sponsors it. A fund that limits applicants' time has an interest in saying this.
- Seibel's evidence is his own Justin.tv and Socialcam experience.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to end it this week. The departing cofounder should give back most of his stock, even the vested part, and both of you should drop the lawyers. The target is a short, no-fault separation with reasonable severance and clean paperwork.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). The 2026 Dalton + Michael cofounder episode ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U) covers pre-PMF breakups, vested stock and lawyers.

**What he'd tell you**
1. **Stop wasting time.** "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 9:26, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=566s); by: seibel; conf: medium)
2. **Stop the letters.** Your stock is worth nothing before PMF, so the lawyers are the only people getting paid.
   - "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." (@ 11:36; by: seibel; conf: medium)
   - "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." (@ 12:07; by: seibel; conf: medium)
3. **Vested stock still goes mostly back.** He argues the company's future value belongs to whoever stays.
   - "the vast majority of the value this company could create hasn't been created yet." (@ 14:47; by: seibel; conf: medium)
   - "Like, you get to hedge. The founder staying doesn't." (@ 15:21; by: seibel; conf: medium)
4. **Aim for these numbers:**
   - "even if you vested, like get down to under 5% of the company, if it's within the first year, under 2%." (@ 18:39; by: seibel; conf: medium)
   - "After a number of years, 5% typical. Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." (@ 21:22; by: seibel; conf: high)

   At 9 months you're in the first-year bracket, so expect something like 1–2% or less. If he leaves with a chunk (say 10–25%), that's far above Seibel's range.
5. **Make the deal in a week for about $2,000.** "Do reasonable severance, sign clean paperwork and and peace out" (@ 18:39). In the same passage he says "you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000."
6. **Whoever stays should be the generous one.** If that's you, he'd say: "it is so cheap to be nice" (@ 17:33), and "understand that everyone in your company is looking at you right now." (@ 17:33). He also says "if you think of yourself as the responsible party and you act that way, often you don't trigger victimness on the other side, too." (@ 18:06). Seibel says he often talks to the departing founder first and makes the case for leaving equity with the team that stays.
7. **Drop the blame.** "If you made a list of all the things we screwed up in our company, it would be way longer than the things you're pissed at your co-founder about." (@ 21:54; by: seibel; conf: high) Caldwell adds: "Don't try to ruin the other person. Don't try to ruin the reputation." (@ 13:42) and "Make it so that you don't say things you can't take back." (@ 14:14)

**What he's done:** He says he often makes the case to the departing founder for leaving equity with the team. He also describes YC's written breakup standards, so every partner gives both cofounders the same advice.

**What would change his answer**
- **Misconduct.** He says: "if your co-founder is breaking the law, doing something unethical, killing people, none of this applies." (@ 21:54)
- **Real value.** His advice assumes the stock is worth little. If the company has real traction or funding, his rationale weakens, though you said it's pre-PMF and "over".
- **Who stays.** The "hedge" argument assumes someone is staying to carry the company. If you're both walking away, there's nothing to protect. He'd still say to settle cheaply and quickly, because the lawyers' fees are the only thing left to lose.
- **Your lawyers.** The vault has nothing on how to unwind letters already sent, or on whether your jurisdiction or vesting agreement changes the legal position. That part is a guess: have your lawyer do the minimum paperwork, and not the negotiating.

**Caveats on the source**
- It's one episode, sponsored by Standard Capital, and most of the quotes are medium-confidence attributions.
- Seibel and Caldwell speak from YC office-hours experience, not as lawyers. Check any real equity agreement with counsel.
- I disagree on one point. A cofounder who holds vested stock isn't obliged to give it back, so Seibel's advice relies on goodwill and on the other person seeing the logic. That is why he says to approach them first, as a peer, not through letters.

**Correction first:** Garry Tan didn't say this. Sam Altman did, in a YC talk with Tan, "Sam Altman: 'Never a Better Time to Do a Startup'" (July 2026). Altman even says "I can say this, Gary probably can't," because Tan runs YC and would have a conflict of interest.

**Verdict:** Altman's reason is network effects. The Bay Area and YC network put the people who might become your co-founders in one place, and that advantage compounds. He says the "distance between like YC and second place has expanded."

**Based on:** said it, though only partly. He gives the network-effects reason but no data or specific mechanism for why the gap has grown.

**Why he'd say it**
- The claim itself: "I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded. And this is a reminder of the power of network effects." (`yt-ZIaOBAjvc38` @ 16:56, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s)
- The context is the co-founder problem. The line comes right after he says YC's old, "heretical" rule to move to San Francisco "was clearly right" because "you got a lot of like lucky chances and collisions." The best way to find your people was to be where the people were.
- His takeaway is about networks, not YC alone: "the sooner you can put yourself just in a flow where you're going to meet the people that will be your eventual co-founders… I think the better," and "it takes a long time to compound." (@ 17:28, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1048s)
- His example is his own history. He met the people he started OpenAI with years before founding it, and he met Greg Brockman by helping Stripe recruit him.
- Tan's added comment is that YC works because of a "loose network and the spirit of helping each other and this like very long-term outlook." (@ 23:35) Tan doesn't make the second-place claim himself.

**What would change the answer:** Altman hedges on the related Bay Area point. He says "I don't know if this is still going to be true for the next 10 years. I suspect it will be," and that he has "less of an intuition for it now." He also admits his conflict of interest, so this is an informed opinion from YC's former president at a YC event, not a measured comparison with other accelerators. The vault has nothing further on why the gap grew, such as AI-era dynamics or specific competitors.

Source leaf: `wiki/hiring/cofounders/finding-cofounders-and-your-people.md`.

Checking the vault turned up the opposite of your premise, so here's the correction first.

**Verdict:** The vault has no record of Jessica Livingston saying early YC backed the most aggressive, ruthless founders because they win. What she says points the other way, so I can't give you her reason for a belief she doesn't hold.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high)

**What she said instead**
- "Aggressive" and "ruthless" appear once in her words, and she uses them about investors, not founders. She contrasts herself with them: "I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless - for a couple of them that I know I cared about how founders were feeling" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 17:44, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s).
- Her screen for founders was character, not toughness. "From the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" (@ 14:51). She also asked "did they seem earnest did they seem determined were they flexible minded and most importantly what was the relationship between the co-founders like."
- She turned down applicants she judged conceited, and says that choice shaped the alumni culture. "Early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" (@ 15:27). She admits YC has since funded some conceited founders.
- "Earnest and not pretentious that's in YC's DNA" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 45:34, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2734s).

**Where your premise may come from**
- She does value toughness in the sense of persistence and independence, not aggression. "You do need a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid and to keep going when you're ridiculed or ignored" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 25:45).
- She also says "you cannot be conventional minded to start a startup with a brand new idea" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 51:09), and that all the founders she's known are "very determined" (@ 51:43).
- Paul Graham (PG) separately says the hardest part of judging founders was predicting how tough and ambitious they'd become. The vault also has his word "formidable", meaning someone who gets what they want in any situation. That is PG's view, not hers, and it doesn't mean ruthless.
- Hardness isn't her stated reason for why founders win. Her stated reasons are character, the co-founder relationship, and making something users want.

**What would change this:** a source where she explicitly praises ruthlessness in founders. I searched the vault for "ruthless", "aggressive" and "relentless" and found nothing like that. If you have a specific talk in mind, point me to it and I'll check it. It may be PG or someone else being attributed to her.

Sources are in `wiki/fundraising/investors/what-yc-looks-for-in-founders.md` and `wiki/thinking/livingston.md`.
